title: Stanford MYCIN Expert System Matches and Outperforms Infectious-Disease Specialists in Blinded JAMA Meningitis Evaluation
whyItMatters: Landmark JAMA blinded trial showing a symbolic AI (~450 backward-chaining rules with certainty factors) outperformed five Stanford infectious-disease faculty specialists on meningitis antimicrobial selection.
summary: Published in JAMA on September 21, 1979, Victor L. Yu, Lawrence M. Fagan, Edward H. Shortliffe, Bruce G. Buchanan, and colleagues at Stanford University conducted a rigorous blinded evaluation of MYCIN against human clinicians on ten complex cases of acute infectious meningitis. Eight independent national infectious-disease experts scored de-identified prescriptions: MYCIN achieved 65% therapeutic acceptability—outscoring every individual Stanford faculty specialist (42.5% to 62.5%), fellows, residents, and actual treating physicians—while never failing to cover a treatable pathogen. MYCIN established certainty-factor reasoning, explainable backward-chaining inference, and rigorous blinded clinical benchmarking for medical AI.
technicalHighlights: Encoded ~450 domain production rules with certainty factors to reason under clinical uncertainty and incomplete lab cultures.
Achieved 65% blinded expert acceptability vs. 42.5%–62.5% for Stanford infectious-disease faculty specialists.
Provided natural-language explanation traces (“why” and “how” queries) justifying every recommended antimicrobial regimen.
caveats: Evaluated on 10 complex retrospective meningitis cases and never deployed into routine hospital care due to 1970s compute/data-entry friction and clinical liability norms.

scoreRationale.foundational: First blinded clinical proof that an AI reasoning system could match or exceed subspecialist physicians on high-stakes diagnostic therapy.
scoreRationale.ripple: Defined the expert-system architecture (eMYCIN, PROSPECTOR) and set the methodological template for modern clinical AI trials.
scoreRationale.verification: Peer-reviewed blinded evaluation published in JAMA (Vol. 242, No. 12, pp. 1279–1282).
scoreRationale.velocity: Real-time consultation on mainframe terminals, though rule engineering required years.
